title: Your secret weapon: break any sentence into carriage, engine and modifiers
summary: Every long sentence is a が carriage and an engine, with everything else telling you more about one of them.

blocks.text: A very long Japanese sentence is usually less complicated than it looks. Every logical clause has just two core parts: the **が main carriage** (visible or zero) and the **engine**. They are not just part of the sentence: **they are the sentence**. Everything else only gives more information about one of them.

Lesson 46 said modifiers go before the noun. The full rule is wider: **anything that modifies anything goes before it**. That includes the engine. In an other-move sentence, the nouns marked by **を, に, で and へ** are all modifiers of the verb: each tells you more about the action. (の is different: it links one noun to another noun.)
Take the sentence below. Its core is only (私が) あげた, "I gave". Everything else answers a question about it.

blocks.jp: （私が）母が焼いたケーキを眼鏡をかけた女の子にあげた。
blocks.en: (I) gave the cake my mother baked to the girl wearing glasses.

blocks.text: Peel the sentence like this: find the final engine, find its carriage, then ask each other piece "what are you telling me more about?" Pieces ending in an engine in front of a noun are simply clauses describing that noun.

A sentence can hold two complete clauses, such as 店に行ってパンを買った ("went to the shop and bought bread"). Both clauses have a carriage, and the second one shares the first one's zero carriage. English does the same with "I went to the shop and bought bread". The more clauses you can recognize, the more manageable long sentences become.

items: Every logical clause is a **carriage + engine**; the rest modifies one of the two.
**を, に, で, へ** nouns modify the verb; **の** links two nouns.
Anything that modifies something stands **before** it.
To read a long sentence: find the engine, find the carriage, then attach each piece.

questions.instruction: What are the two core parts of a sentence?
options: The が carriage and the engine

questions.instruction: What do を, に, で and へ nouns do in a verb sentence?
questions.note: They tell us more about the action.

questions.instruction: Which particle links one noun to another?
questions.note: の couples nouns; it does not describe the verb.
買った ends the clause and carries the action.

questions.instruction: Tap the part that describes ケーキ
questions.note: A clause in front of a noun describes it.

questions.instruction: In 駅で友達に会った, which part modifies the verb with a place?
questions.note: で gives the place of the action.

questions.instruction: What does 友達に tell you in the same sentence?
questions.note: に marks the person the action reached.

questions.prompt: In 眼鏡をかけた女の子, the part 眼鏡をかけた describes 女の子.
questions.note: It ends in an engine and comes before the noun.

questions.instruction: Which part of this sentence is in the zero carriage?
questions.prompt: 店に行ってパンを買った。
options: The person who went and bought
questions.note: Both clauses share the same zero carriage.

questions.prompt: (I) read the book my friend lent me.
questions.note: The clause 友達が貸した describes 本; then the engine closes the sentence.

questions.instruction: How many logical clauses are in this sentence?
questions.prompt: 朝起きて、顔を洗って、コーヒーを飲んだ。
questions.note: 起きて, 洗って and 飲んだ each have their own action.

questions.instruction: What is the best first step with a very long sentence?
options: Find the final engine and its carriage
questions.note: The core is the sentence; everything else attaches to it.
